paras: The killing of Trinnell Ellis was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Julian Beckett, a member of a posse led by Marshal Tom Crawford, during a midnight raid on a gambling game at Thunderbolt, Georgia, on the night of August 22, 1903. A second Black man, Eddie West, was wounded in the arm by the marshal's fire and escaped. Recorder L. W. Nelson exonerated Beckett two days later, while the men caught in the house were bound over to the City Court for gambling. The Savannah Morning News told the story entirely from the posse's side.

About midnight on Saturday, August 22, Crawford was told that "half a dozen or more negroes" were gambling in a shack near Bannon Lodge. The marshal organized a posse, and Beckett, a young man connected with the Warsaw Ice and Light Company, answered the call along with a Capt. Parker.

The posse surrounded the shack and closed in on the men, who were playing the card game "skin," and when the command to halt was given they scattered. Crawford, posted at the rear, said the men ran out a back door, that one of them fired at him, and that the lights went out as four or five disappeared into a heavy growth of coffee weeds. He fired four times, and one bullet struck Eddie West in the arm, but West kept running and had not been arrested by August 24.

Ellis went out the front and had reached the road when Beckett shot him. By Beckett's account, Ellis wrenched a picket from the fence and turned on him with it raised, "applying a vile epithet," and Beckett fired "in defense of his life." Ellis was hit in the leg and in the head, the fatal bullet entering his mouth and leaving at the back of his skull. The coverage contains no account from Ellis's companions or any other Black witness.

Recorder Nelson notified Coroner Keller, who went to Thunderbolt the next morning and left the matter to the town's authorities; no report of an inquest appears in the coverage. Beckett was not locked up and spent the day at his company's plant, while Ellis's body was turned over to his sister for burial. On August 24 Nelson heard statements from Crawford, Parker and Beckett and from Dr. McGee, who had examined the wounds, found "not the slightest conflict in the evidence," and dismissed Beckett.

The men held from the raid were given a hearing at Thunderbolt on August 25 and bound over to the City Court. On August 28 Anderson Kelly was to be tried there for running a gaming house and Joe Spellman for gambling. The coverage does not show the outcome of those cases or whether West was ever arrested.

All of the reporting found came from the Savannah Morning News, which carried the story on August 23, 24, 25, 26 and 28; no Black-press report was found. Its headlines put Ellis's alleged attack first, "NEGRO ARMED WITH PICKETT KILLED BY JULIAN BECKETT," and announced the result of the hearing as "BECKETT JUSTIFIED IN KILLING ELLIS." The paper called the shooter "Mr. Beckett" and "the young man," while it described Ellis as "a dangerous negro" who had been "well known to the authorities."

Its first report ended by recalling that Ellis had once been arrested with a white woman and sentenced to the chaingang, and that the woman later killed herself. The account of the shooting came from Beckett and Crawford, and the paper noted that their statements at the hearing were "in accord with the facts given in the Morning News."

The first report's subheading named the victim "Grinnell Ellis," while its text and every later report gave "Trinnell." The first report said the head wound "caused instant death," but the next day's paper said Ellis lived about thirty minutes and made no statement. Crawford's charge that a gambler fired first appeared only in the second report and rests on his word alone. The men held were named Joe Spaulding, Anderson Tyler and Isaac Brown on August 24, but Joseph Spellman, Isaac Brown and Andrew Talley on August 26.

reader.title: Killing of Trinnell Ellis
bases: A posse organized by Marshal Tom Crawford raided a gambling game, and one of its members, Julian Beckett, shot and killed Trinnell Ellis while the marshal wounded Eddie West (A1, A2).

Ellis was killed by a member of a posse of at least three (Crawford, Parker, Beckett) acting under the town marshal during a gambling raid, and the recorder ruled the shooting justified (A1, A2, A3); the coverage shows a posse shooting during an attempted arrest under official authority, not a group killing outside the law, though the only account is the posse's own.
All five reports come from one paper, the Savannah Morning News, and rest on the statements of Beckett and Marshal Crawford (A1, A2, A3); no independent or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Julian Beckett
accounts.gist: Ellis jumped from the house, wrenched a picket from the fence and came at him with it raised, cursing him, and he fired in defense of his life.

accounts.label: Marshal Crawford
accounts.gist: The men fled through a rear door, one fired at him and the lights were blown out; he fired four times as they ran into the coffee weeds, wounding West.

accounts.label: Recorder's investigation
accounts.gist: Statements of Crawford, Parker and Beckett agreed with the paper's account; Ellis was found to have been advancing with a picket, and Beckett was dismissed.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined "NEGRO ARMED WITH PICKETT KILLED BY JULIAN BECKETT" and "BECKETT JUSTIFIED IN KILLING ELLIS," gave Beckett's account as fact, called Ellis "a dangerous negro," and recounted his past arrest with a white woman.
